_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 3 Computing unit lecture film, Lesson 3 Think It Through. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The chapters follow LESSON[lecture] in order: logical thinking, predicting a change (the smoothie, then the kite), dividing a big task into sections, why sections are easier to follow and to edit, and a decision. Every changed algorithm is drawn by handing the lesson's OWN scene the changed list - ART.scene(smoothie, [banana, berries, milk, blend]) and ART.scene(kite, [sticks, tie, paper, tail, fly]) - so the kit paints the splattered kitchen and the lost kite and writes its own caption. The film draws no picture of a wrong outcome of its own.
title: Think It Through
subtitle: Grade 3 Computing
objectives: Know that logical thinking is used in the creation of algorithms.
Predict the outcome of a change to an algorithm that is presented as a sequence of steps.
Know that many tasks can be divided into smaller sections to make them easier to follow and to edit.

beats.say: Swap two steps in an algorithm. What will happen? You can work it out.
Think it through. Every step has a reason, and a big task divides into sections.
Every step in a good algorithm is there for a reason.
Boil the water, then pour it, because you pour boiling water.
Toast the bread, then butter it. Butter in a toaster would melt and burn.
Unlock the door, then open it, because a locked door does not open.
That reasoning is logical thinking. It is how algorithms are created.
Here is the smoothie algorithm from lesson one. Six steps in order.
Now make one change. Swap the lid step and the blending step.
Before you watch, predict. What happens when the blender starts?
The blender runs with no lid on, and the smoothie sprays everywhere.
The same thinking on another task. Here is the kite algorithm.
Swap the string step and the running step. Predict what will happen.
You run into the wind, and nothing holds the kite. The wind takes it.
Take the tail step out instead: a kite with no tail, and nothing else changes.
Getting ready for school is one big task. Ten steps in one long list.
One long list is hard to follow, and hard to edit.
So divide it into sections: wash, dress, breakfast, bag.
Every step goes into one section. Teeth into wash. Shirt into dress.
Four short lists instead of one long one. Each section is a sub-task.

scenes.heading: Easier to follow, easier to edit

beats.say: Sections are easier to follow. Each one is short, so you know where you are.
They are easier to edit. Change breakfast from cereal to toast.
Wash, dress and bag do not change at all. A change stays in its section.
If you are late, you can ask which section took too long.
Logical thinking is mostly about decisions.
A decision is a point where a question decides what happens next.
Is it raining? Then take a coat. If it is not, you do not.
You make dozens of decisions a day. Writing one down makes it an algorithm.
Logic puts every step where it is, for a reason.
Predict what a change will do before you make it.
Divide a big task into small sections. Each one is a sub-task.
A decision sends an algorithm one way or the other. Think it through.
